title: Energy Communities Leadership Seminar Powering Change for Rural Youth in Europe
summary: Introduction: Rural Youth and the Energy Transition The energy transition in Europe is one of the most ambitious societal transformations of our time. It is not only about shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources but also about rethinking how communities organize, govern, and sustain themselves. At the heart of this transformation lies the concept of energy communities — local, citizen‑led initiatives that empower people to take control of their energy future. Rural areas, often marginalized in national policy debates, are uniquely positioned to benefit from and contribute to this transition. They are rich in renewable resources such as wind, solar, and biomass, yet they face persistent challenges: limited infrastructure, energy poverty, geographic isolation, and reduced political influence. These challenges can make rural communities feel excluded from the broader energy transition. However, rural youth represent a powerful force for change. They are deeply connected to their communities, understand local realities, and bring creativity, resilience, and innovation to problem‑solving. Yet, many lack access to the training, networks, and resources necessary to lead energy initiatives. Without targeted support, their potential remains untapped. This is where Rural Youth Europe (RYE) steps in. Through the Powering Change – Empowering Rural Youth for Energy Communities project , RYE is committed to equipping young people with the knowledge, skills, and partnerships needed to establish and support local energy communities. The flagship event of this initiative is the Capacity‑Building Seminar on Energy Communities , scheduled for 1–4 November 2026 in Bilbao, Spain . This seminar is not just another conference. It is a transformative experience designed to empower 25 motivated young participants from across Europe. Over three days, they will learn from experts, engage in interactive workshops, and collaborate with peers to explore the practical aspects of developing energy communities in rural areas. The seminar will strengthen their capacity to become local leaders of the energy transition, capable of building community‑led energy initiatives that are sustainable, inclusive, and impactful. About the Seminar The seminar is designed as an immersive, multi‑day experience where participants move beyond theory into practice. Dates: 1–4 November 2026 Location: Bilbao, Spain — a city known for innovation and sustainability. Organizers: Rural Youth Europe (RYE), a network dedicated to empowering rural youth. Participants: 25 selected young people from diverse European countries and rural contexts. The seminar will blend expert lectures with interactive workshops, peer learning, and collaborative project design. Participants will explore governance models, financing strategies, technical solutions, and community engagement approaches. The emphasis is on practical application — equipping participants with tools they can take back to their communities. Objectives of the Seminar Knowledge Development Provide a comprehensive overview of energy communities, their role in Europe’s energy transition, and the unique challenges faced by rural areas. Explore European policy frameworks supporting community energy initiatives. Skill Building Train participants in project management, stakeholder engagement, and technical planning. Offer hands‑on exercises in designing energy community models. Networking and Partnerships Facilitate connections among participants, experts, and practitioners. Encourage cross‑border collaborations that extend beyond the seminar. Leadership Empowerment Strengthen the capacity of rural youth to become local leaders of the energy transition. Inspire participants to initiate or support energy projects in their home regions. Structure of the Seminar Day 1: Setting the Stage Introduction to energy communities and Europe’s energy transition. Keynote lectures from experts in sustainable energy and rural development. Ice‑breaking activities to build trust and connections among participants. Day 2: Practical Skills and Case Studies Workshops on governance, financing, and technical solutions. Case studies of successful energy communities in rural Europe. Group discussions on challenges and opportunities in participants’ home regions. Day 3: Collaborative Action Peer learning sessions where participants share their own experiences. Collaborative activities to design mock energy community projects. Closing plenary to reflect on lessons learned and plan next steps. Benefits of Participation Acquire practical skills to establish or support local energy communities. Learn directly from experienced practitioners and experts. Connect with peers from across Europe, building lasting networks. Contribute to Europe’s energy transition by becoming a local leader. Participate in a transformative experience that combines learning, collaboration, and action. Gain visibility within Rural Youth Europe’s network and beyond. Application Details Deadline: Applications must be submitted before 1 November 2026 . Eligibility: Open to motivated young people from across Europe, particularly those from rural communities. Selection Criteria: Motivation, commitment, and potential to contribute to the energy transition. Number of Participants: 25 selected individuals. Process: Applicants submit a form detailing their background, motivation, and interest in energy communities. Apply HERE today! FAQs 1. What exactly is an energy community, and why does it matter? An energy community is a collective initiative where citizens, businesses, and local organizations collaborate to produce, consume, and manage renewable energy. These communities democratize energy production, reduce costs, and promote sustainability. They matter because they empower people to take control of their energy future, foster social cohesion, and contribute to Europe’s climate goals. 2. Who can apply for the seminar? The seminar is open to motivated young people from across Europe, particularly those from rural areas. Applicants should have a passion for sustainability, community development, and energy transition. No prior technical expertise is required; what matters most is motivation, commitment, and a willingness to learn. 3. What will participants gain from the seminar? Participants will acquire knowledge about energy communities, practical skills for project development, and insights into governance, financing, and technical solutions. They will also build networks with peers and experts, gain visibility within Rural Youth Europe’s network, and return to their communities equipped to initiate or support energy projects. 4. How many participants will be selected, and how? A total of 25 motivated young people will be chosen. Selection will be based on motivation, commitment, and potential to contribute to the energy transition. Diversity will be prioritized to ensure representation from different countries, rural contexts, and backgrounds. 5. Is there a cost to attend? Details about costs, travel, and accommodation will be provided by Rural Youth Europe. The seminar is designed to be accessible, with efforts made to minimize financial barriers for participants. 6. Why was Bilbao, Spain chosen as the location? Bilbao is a city with a strong commitment to sustainability and innovation. It has undergone a remarkable transformation from an industrial hub to a modern, vibrant city known for its cultural and environmental initiatives. Hosting the seminar in Bilbao underscores the importance of innovation and resilience in the energy transition. 7. What is the long‑term impact of the seminar? The seminar is designed to have lasting effects. Participants will return to their communities equipped with knowledge, skills, and networks to initiate or support energy projects. They will become ambassadors of the energy transition, inspiring others and contributing to Europe’s broader climate goals. 8. How does this seminar connect to Europe’s policy goals? The seminar aligns with the European Union’s emphasis on citizen‑led energy initiatives and rural development. By empowering rural youth, it supports the EU’s goals of inclusivity, sustainability, and resilience in the energy transition. 9. What makes this seminar unique compared to other training programs? Unlike generic training programs, this seminar is tailored specifically to rural youth. It combines expert knowledge with peer learning, emphasizes practical application, and fosters cross‑border collaboration. It is not just about learning; it is about empowering participants to act. To learn more about the Energy Communities Leadership Seminar HERE. Conclusion The Capacity‑Building Seminar on Energy Communities is more than an event; it is a movement. It represents a commitment to empowering rural youth to become active contributors to Europe’s energy transition. By providing knowledge, skills, and partnerships, the seminar equips young people to build community‑led energy initiatives that are sustainable, inclusive, and impactful. Taking place from 1–4 November 2026 in Bilbao, Spain , the seminar will bring together 25 motivated young participants from across Europe. Through interactive workshops, peer learning, and collaborative activities, participants will strengthen their capacity to become local leaders of the energy transition. The seminar’s impact will extend far beyond its three days. Participants will return to their communities as catalysts for change, initiating projects, inspiring others, and contributing to a future where everyone has access to clean, affordable energy. They will embody the values of resilience, innovation, and collaboration that are essential for the energy transition. In conclusion, the seminar is not just about learning; it is about action. It is about equipping rural youth with the tools they need to drive change in their communities, to build energy systems that are fair and sustainable, and to contribute to a future where Europe’s energy transition is not only technological but also social, inclusive, and just. title: PhD Position in Urban Health Equity 2026: Heat Risks, Pediatric Respiratory Health and Greenspace Interventions at the University of Amsterdam
summary: Introduction: Climate Change, Urban Health, and Equity Climate change is not a distant abstraction; it is a lived reality shaping the daily experiences of millions of people across the globe. Cities, as hubs of human activity, are particularly vulnerable to its impacts. The urban heat island effect intensifies heat waves, raising temperatures in built environments far above those in surrounding rural areas. This phenomenon is compounded by environmental degradation, air pollution, and socio‑economic inequalities, creating a perfect storm of health risks. Children are among the most vulnerable groups in this context. Their respiratory systems are still developing, making them highly sensitive to pollutants, aeroallergens, and extreme heat exposure. Research consistently shows that heat events correlate with increased asthma rates, exacerbations of chronic respiratory conditions, and long‑term reductions in lung function. These health challenges do not exist in isolation; they ripple outward, influencing educational achievement, social participation, and future socio‑economic attainment. The University of Amsterdam (UvA) has recognized the urgency of addressing these interconnected challenges. Through its Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences, UvA is offering a PhD position focused on Urban Health Equity and the Impacts of Heat Risks . This project is not merely academic; it is a call to action. By bridging biomedical sciences and urban studies, the research will explore how rising temperatures intersect with pediatric respiratory health and how urban greenspace interventions can serve as a pathway toward health equity. This PhD position is embedded in a broader vision: to understand the lived realities of marginalized urban populations, to connect scientific evidence with socio‑political contexts, and to generate actionable insights that can inform urban planning and public health policy. It is an opportunity to contribute to cutting‑edge interdisciplinary research that has both local relevance in Amsterdam Southeast and global significance in the fight for climate justice and health equity. Project Overview: Urban Greenspaces and Health Urban greenspaces are increasingly recognized as vital components of climate adaptation strategies. Parks, gardens, and green corridors can reduce local temperatures, improve air quality, and provide psychological and social benefits. Yet, the relationship between greenspaces and health is far from straightforward. Unequal distribution : Greenspaces are often concentrated in affluent neighborhoods, leaving marginalized communities with limited access. This unequal distribution perpetuates health disparities. Historical disinvestment : Many urban planning decisions have systematically neglected disadvantaged districts, amplifying inequities. Amsterdam Southeast, for example, has faced decades of underinvestment, making it a critical site for examining how new greenspaces can reshape health outcomes. Climate vs. health planning : Greenspaces are often designed to mitigate climate risks, such as reducing heat, but they do not automatically translate into improved health outcomes. The challenge lies in aligning climate adaptation strategies with public health goals. This PhD project will explore these dynamics in depth, focusing on Amsterdam Southeast and the newly created Nelson Mandelapark . By combining biomedical explanations (individual interactions with the environment as causes of disease) with urban political ecological explanations (socio‑political conditions shaping environments and institutions), the research will provide a holistic understanding of how greenspaces can promote health equity. Research Objectives The PhD candidate will undertake a series of interconnected research tasks designed to capture the complexity of urban health equity: Quantitative Vulnerability and Risk Assessment Map hydro‑meteorologic and pediatric respiratory health risks. Use intersectionality as a lens to understand how social identities (such as race, class, and gender) shape heat risk experiences. Combine mechanistic pathway mapping (secondary data on environmental stressors and respiratory outcomes) with qualitative interviews to capture lived experiences. Qualitative Examination of Urban Greenspace Planning Investigate dominant planning and management regimes. Conduct interviews with caregivers, residents, and public officials to understand how greening strategies intersect with health and climate change adaptation. Explore how policies and institutions shape access to greenspaces. Integrated Multi‑Scalar Analysis Link bodily experiences of heat exposure with political‑economic systems. Examine how urban environments shape pediatric respiratory health at multiple scales, from individual bodies to citywide planning regimes. Ranking and Prioritization of Greenspace Interventions Assess existing interventions in Amsterdam Southeast. Provide recommendations for future urban planning strategies that prioritize health equity. This multi‑layered approach ensures that the research captures both the biological mechanisms of disease and the socio‑political contexts that shape health outcomes. Supervisors and Institutional Context The PhD candidate will be supervised by: Dr Jannes Willems (Urban Planning, Department of Geography, Planning and International Development Studies) Dr Vanessa Harris (Department of Global Health, Amsterdam University Medical Centers) Prof Maria Kaika (Urban Studies and Political Ecology) The candidate will be embedded in the Urban Planning research group at UvA and affiliated with the Department of Global Health at Amsterdam UMC . This dual affiliation ensures a truly interdisciplinary environment, combining social science and biomedical expertise. Candidate Requirements Applicants should hold a (Research) Master’s degree in one or more of the following fields: Human geography Urban and regional planning Urban studies Public health Global health Medicine (MD) Biomedical sciences Environmental studies Interdisciplinary programs bridging these fields Preferred qualifications include: Experience conducting fieldwork in unfamiliar settings, demonstrating adaptability and resilience. Familiarity with mixed methods research, combining qualitative and quantitative approaches. Strong writing skills and ability to develop complex, critical arguments. Excellent English proficiency (written and verbal). Dutch language skills (preferred, for fieldwork in Amsterdam Southeast). Ability to work independently while also contributing to collaborative research teams. The ideal candidate will be passionate about interdisciplinary research, committed to social justice, and eager to contribute to innovative solutions at the intersection of climate adaptation, public health, and urban equity. Benefits and Opportunities Successful candidates will enjoy a range of benefits and opportunities: Interdisciplinary supervision : A supportive team of supervisors from both social science and biomedical backgrounds. International research networks : Opportunities to attend conferences, workshops, and seminars, connecting with scholars worldwide. Resources for fieldwork : Funding and logistical support for conducting research in Amsterdam Southeast. Professional development : Access to courses and training through the Amsterdam Institute for Social Science Research. Collaborative environment : Embedding in two leading research groups (Urban Planning and Global Health) that value curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking. This combination of resources and support ensures that the PhD candidate can thrive academically while also contributing to meaningful societal change. Application Process Applications must include: Curriculum vitae (with contact details for two references). Motivation letter (max 750 words), outlining your interest in the project and your suitability for the role. Research statement (max 500 words), sharing your initial ideas on how to approach the project. Writing sample in English (article, thesis chapter, or assignment). Deadline: Applications close on 9 August 2026 . Interviews: Week of 7 September 2026 (preferably in person in Amsterdam). Start date: 1 November 2026. For inquiries, contact: Dr Jannes Willems (j.j.willems@uva.nl) Dr Vanessa Harris (v.c.harris@amsterdamumc.nl) Apply HERE today! FAQs 1. What is the central focus of this PhD project? The project investigates how rising temperatures and environmental degradation affect pediatric respiratory health, particularly in marginalized urban communities. It also explores how urban greenspace interventions can mitigate these impacts. The research is designed to connect biomedical explanations (individual interactions with the environment as causes of disease) with urban political ecological explanations (socio‑political conditions shaping environments and institutions). 2. Where will the research be conducted? Fieldwork will take place in Amsterdam Southeast , with a particular focus on the newly created Nelson Mandelapark . This location is significant because it represents both a site of new greenspace development and a community that has historically faced socio‑economic challenges. 3. What disciplines are relevant for applicants? Applicants from a wide range of disciplines are encouraged to apply, including human geography, urban and regional planning, urban studies, public health, global health, medicine, biomedical sciences, and environmental studies. Interdisciplinary backgrounds that bridge these fields are especially valued. 4. Is Dutch language proficiency required? While Dutch proficiency is not mandatory, it is highly preferred. Fieldwork will involve engaging with caregivers, residents, and public officials in Amsterdam Southeast, many of whom may be more comfortable communicating in Dutch. Having this skill will enhance the depth and authenticity of the research. 5. What is the application deadline? Applications close on 9 August 2026 . This deadline is firm, and candidates are encouraged to prepare their materials well in advance to ensure timely submission. 6. When will interviews be held? Interviews are scheduled for the week of 7 September 2026 , preferably in person in Amsterdam. This provides an opportunity for candidates to meet the supervision team and gain a deeper understanding of the research environment. 7. What is the expected start date? The preferred start date is 1 November 2026 . This allows sufficient time for onboarding, preparation, and integration into the research groups at UvA and Amsterdam UMC. 8. What kind of support will the PhD candidate receive? The candidate will benefit from an enthusiastic and warm interdisciplinary supervision team, access to international research networks, resources for fieldwork, and professional development opportunities through the Amsterdam Institute for Social Science Research. 9. How does this project contribute to broader societal goals? By focusing on pediatric respiratory health and greenspace interventions, the project addresses urgent societal challenges related to climate adaptation, public health, and social justice. The findings will have implications not only for Amsterdam but also for cities worldwide grappling with similar issues. To learn more about the PhD Position Urban Health Equity click HERE. Conclusion This PhD position at the University of Amsterdam is more than an academic opportunity; it is a chance to contribute to transformative research at the intersection of climate change, urban health, and equity. The project recognizes that children are at the frontline of climate impacts, and that their health outcomes are deeply intertwined with socio‑economic conditions and urban environments. By investigating how rising temperatures and environmental degradation affect pediatric respiratory health, and by exploring the potential of greenspace interventions, the research aims to generate actionable insights that can inform urban planning, public health policy, and climate adaptation strategies. The University of Amsterdam offers a supportive, interdisciplinary environment where curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking are valued. Candidates who are passionate about interdisciplinary research, committed to social justice, and eager to contribute to innovative solutions are strongly encouraged to apply. The deadline for applications is 9 August 2026 , with interviews scheduled for the week of 7 September 2026 and a preferred start date of 1 November 2026 . This timeline ensures that the selected candidate can begin their journey at UvA with clarity and purpose. In conclusion, this PhD position represents a unique opportunity to engage in research that is both academically rigorous and socially impactful. It is an invitation to join a community of scholars dedicated to addressing some of the most pressing challenges of our time, and to contribute to a vision of healthier, more equitable, and more resilient cities. title: David Sainsbury International MSc Scholarships 2026/27: Fully Funded and 50% Tuition Scholarships for the MSc in Global Plant Health at the University of East Anglia
summary: The David Sainsbury International MSc Scholarships 2026/27 provide an exceptional opportunity for talented students from around the world to pursue a postgraduate degree in Global Plant Health at the University of East Anglia (UEA), United Kingdom. Hosted by The Sainsbury Laboratory (TSL), these prestigious scholarships are designed to support the next generation of scientists committed to tackling one of the world s most pressing agricultural challenges plant disease. The scholarship programme offers both fully funded scholarships and 50% tuition fee scholarships to outstanding applicants based on their country of residence and economic classification. Through this initiative, The Sainsbury Laboratory aims to build global scientific capacity by equipping future researchers and professionals with advanced knowledge and practical skills to improve global food security, sustainable agriculture, and plant health. It is important to note that all Full Scholarships for entry in 2026 have already been allocated , while a limited number of 50% Fee Scholarships remain available for eligible applicants. About the David Sainsbury International MSc Scholarships The David Sainsbury International MSc Scholarships are funded directly by The Sainsbury Laboratory (TSL) to enable exceptional students to study the MSc in Global Plant Health at the University of East Anglia. The scholarship programme is intended to remove financial barriers for talented students while encouraging graduates to use their expertise to combat plant diseases and strengthen agricultural systems across the world. The programme supports students through either: A Full MSc Scholarship A 50% Tuition Fee Scholarship Scholarship awards are highly competitive and are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis among eligible candidates who satisfy all academic and scholarship requirements. Why Global Plant Health Matters Plant diseases threaten food production, biodiversity, economic growth, and environmental sustainability across the globe. Millions of people depend on healthy crops for food security and income generation. The MSc in Global Plant Health prepares graduates to develop innovative scientific solutions that address these challenges through research, biotechnology, genetics, molecular biology, bioinformatics, and plant pathology. Graduates are expected to become leaders capable of improving agriculture both nationally and internationally. Scholarship Types Available 1. David Sainsbury Full MSc Scholarship The Full Scholarship is intended primarily for applicants from least-developed, low-income, and lower-middle-income countries. This scholarship covers nearly every major cost associated with studying in the UK. Benefits of the Full Scholarship Successful applicants may receive funding covering: Full tuition fees (up to £36,000 for the 2026/27 academic year) Monthly maintenance allowance (to be confirmed; based on the UKRI postgraduate stipend, which was £20,780 in 2025/26) Up to £4,000 for economy-class travel expenses upon submission of valid receipts Financial support for living costs throughout the programme Payments for tuition fees are made directly by The Sainsbury Laboratory to the University of East Anglia. Maintenance grants are paid monthly in advance to scholarship recipients. Travel reimbursements are processed after valid receipts are submitted. Full Scholarship Eligibility Requirements Applicants must satisfy all of the following: Hold an offer of admission to the UEA MSc in Global Plant Health. Be a national of or permanently domiciled in a least-developed, low-income, or lower-middle-income country according to the applicable OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) list. Successfully complete the admission interview. Meet all academic admission requirements. Submit a convincing Statement of Intent outlining plans to return to their home country within five years after graduation to contribute towards solving plant disease challenges. Commitment After Graduation Recipients of the Full Scholarship are expected to return to their country of origin within five years after completing their studies. Graduates are encouraged to contribute to: Agricultural development Scientific research Food security Plant disease management National economic development Community advancement The scholarship therefore represents both financial support and an investment in scientific development across low- and middle-income countries. 2. David Sainsbury 50% Fee Scholarship Applicants from upper-middle-income countries and high-income countries—including the United Kingdom—are automatically considered for the David Sainsbury 50% Fee Scholarship. Benefits of the 50% Fee Scholarship Recipients receive: 50% reduction of tuition fees Tuition support for either Home or International tuition rates Direct payment of scholarship funds to the University For the 2026/27 academic year, the scholarship covers: 50% of the £16,000 Home tuition fee, or 50% of the £36,000 International tuition fee Any existing scholarships exceeding 50% of tuition may affect the value of this award. Eligibility for the 50% Fee Scholarship Applicants must: Hold an offer for the MSc in Global Plant Health. Be from an upper-middle-income or high-income country. Meet all admission requirements. Successfully complete the interview process. Submit the required Statement of Intent after receiving an offer. How Scholarship Selection Works There is no separate scholarship application . Every eligible applicant who applies for admission to the MSc programme before the admission deadline published by UEA is automatically considered. The scholarship selection process includes: Submission of the MSc application to UEA. Academic evaluation. Interview. Formal offer of admission. Submission of a Statement of Intent. Review by the Scholarship Selection Panel. Scholarship offer to successful applicants. Selection Criteria Scholarships are awarded based on several factors, including: Academic excellence Previous academic awards Scientific knowledge Research experience Laboratory skills Understanding of molecular biology Genetics Plant health research Molecular interactions Bioinformatics Statistics Independent research ability Overall potential to contribute to solving plant disease challenges The Statement of Intent also plays a significant role in determining scholarship recipients. Statement of Intent Requirements Eligible applicants will be invited to prepare a written Statement of Intent. Applicants from low- and middle-income countries must explain: How they intend to return home after graduation. How they will use their education to address plant diseases. How they will contribute to scientific advancement and agriculture. Applicants from higher-income countries should describe: How they plan to contribute towards addressing plant disease challenges in low- and middle-income countries. Scholarship Expectations Successful scholars are expected to: Maintain excellent academic performance. Pass every module. Participate actively throughout the programme. Live within reasonable commuting distance of The Sainsbury Laboratory. Attend induction and welcome events. Maintain communication with TSL. Follow the TSL Scientific Integrity Policy. Follow the TSL Code of Personal Conduct. Remain in good financial standing with the University. Situations That May Lead to Scholarship Withdrawal The scholarship may be withdrawn if a student: Is expelled, suspended, or excluded. Provides false information. Commits fraud or dishonesty. Violates TSL ethics or integrity policies. Fails to attend required induction events. Demonstrates poor academic performance. Fails any module. Does not maintain financial obligations with the University. Receives undisclosed funding from another scholarship. Fails to cooperate with required scholarship communications. If withdrawn, recipients may be required to repay tuition fees, maintenance grants, and any other scholarship funds already received. Scholarship Deferral Policy Scholarship awards cannot be deferred . Applicants who postpone admission must compete again for scholarships available in the following academic year. Receiving a scholarship in one year does not guarantee funding in a later year. Marketing and Ambassador Responsibilities Scholarship recipients agree to participate in reasonable promotional activities organised by TSL and UEA. These activities may include: Student testimonials Interviews Photography Public speaking Blogging Social media participation Open Day events Supporting prospective students Recipients are also expected to complete a testimonial at the end of the programme explaining how the scholarship supported their career development. Scholarship Payment Schedule The scholarship is administered as follows: Tuition fees are paid directly to UEA by The Sainsbury Laboratory. Maintenance grants are paid monthly. Travel expenses are reimbursed upon submission of valid economy-class travel receipts. Tuition payments are generally made in three instalments during the academic year. Important Scholarship Conditions Applicants should note that: Scholarships are limited in number. Awards depend on available funding. The Scholarship Panel reserves the right not to make an award if no candidate meets the required standard. Scholarship terms may change before the application deadline provided applicants are not disadvantaged. Applicants remain responsible for paying tuition deposits and fees until a scholarship is officially awarded. Scholarship recipients must complete the University registration process by the required deadline. Acceptance of the scholarship requires signing and submitting the Scholarship Agreement Form before the specified acceptance deadline. Deadline Applicants must submit their application for admission to the MSc in Global Plant Health before the official application deadline published on the University of East Anglia website. The scholarship terms do not specify an exact application deadline. Since scholarship consideration is automatic, applicants are strongly encouraged to apply as early as possible because scholarships are limited and awarded competitively. To learn more about this opportunity and apply click HERE Conclusion The David Sainsbury International MSc Scholarships represent one of the leading opportunities for aspiring plant scientists who wish to develop advanced expertise in Global Plant Health while studying at one of the United Kingdom s respected research institutions. Whether through the fully funded scholarship for applicants from least-developed, low-income, and lower-middle-income countries or the 50% Fee Scholarship for applicants from higher-income countries, the programme is designed to develop highly skilled professionals capable of addressing plant diseases that threaten global agriculture and food security.With no separate scholarship application required, eligible students simply need to apply for admission to the MSc in Global Plant Health at the University of East Anglia before the official admissions deadline. Selection is based on academic excellence, scientific potential, interview performance, and a clear commitment to applying acquired knowledge to solve plant disease challenges worldwide. Applicants interested in this prestigious opportunity should prepare a strong application early, as scholarship places are limited and awarded on a competitive basis. title: MIT School Access and Quality Fellowship 2026–2027: One-Year Fellowship for Education Leaders Advancing Equitable School Access and AI-Driven Education Policy
summary: Applications are now open for the MIT School Access and Quality (SAQ) Fellowship 2026–2027 , a prestigious one-year professional development programme designed for education leaders committed to improving educational equity through more effective school enrollment and school performance policies. Hosted by Blueprint Labs at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) , the fellowship brings together leaders from public school districts, state education agencies, charter management organizations, and nonprofit organizations to learn from leading researchers, policy experts, and fellow practitioners. Through a combination of in-person and virtual programming, participants develop the knowledge, practical skills, and professional network needed to build more equitable, transparent, and efficient education systems. As technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) increasingly influence education policy and school enrollment systems, the fellowship also explores how these emerging tools can be used responsibly to improve educational equity while ensuring that all students and families have fair access to high-quality schools. Applications are open until 24 August 2026 at 5:00 PM ET . About the MIT School Access and Quality (SAQ) Fellowship The MIT School Access and Quality Fellowship is an intensive leadership programme focused on helping education professionals strengthen school enrollment systems and improve school performance policies. The fellowship recognizes that equitable enrollment practices and fair school performance measures are essential for ensuring that every child—regardless of background, geography, race, or socioeconomic status—has access to quality education. Rather than offering purely theoretical instruction, the fellowship combines research, policy discussions, peer learning, and practical problem-solving to help participants implement evidence-based solutions within their own organizations and communities. Throughout the year, Fellows engage directly with: MIT researchers Education policy experts Enrollment specialists School system leaders Fellow practitioners from across the United States The programme creates a collaborative learning environment where participants share experiences, exchange ideas, and develop practical strategies to improve educational outcomes. Why the School Access and Quality Fellowship Matters Across the United States, education systems are experiencing significant challenges. These include: Declining student enrollment Persistent educational inequities Unequal access to high-performing schools Family disengagement Inconsistent school performance measures Increasing complexity in enrollment systems Growing use of Artificial Intelligence in educational decision-making Many school districts and education organizations lack sufficient resources or evidence-based guidance to redesign enrollment systems in ways that improve fairness and educational access. The MIT SAQ Fellowship addresses these challenges by equipping education leaders with research-backed strategies, collaborative learning opportunities, and practical tools that can strengthen enrollment policies while keeping equity at the center of decision-making. Fellowship Objectives The programme aims to help education leaders build stronger, fairer, and more effective school systems. By the end of the fellowship, participants will be better prepared to: Improve educational equity Design better enrollment policies Strengthen school performance systems Build trust with families and communities Improve decision-making through research Apply Artificial Intelligence responsibly within education Collaborate across different education sectors Lead evidence-based policy reforms What Fellows Will Learn The fellowship curriculum focuses on contemporary issues affecting school access and education policy. Participants will explore topics including: 1. Improving Educational Equity Fellows learn how enrollment policies can promote: Fair school access Equal opportunities Inclusive education Better student outcomes 2. Family and Community Engagement Participants examine strategies for: Working effectively with families Building stakeholder trust Encouraging community participation Improving communication 3. Artificial Intelligence in Education A distinctive component of the fellowship is its focus on AI. Participants learn how AI can be used to: Forecast school enrollment Evaluate enrollment policies Improve education planning Support evidence-based decisions The programme also considers important questions regarding: Equity Accessibility Responsible AI Family experiences with AI-driven school choice systems 4. Data-Driven Decision Making Participants strengthen their ability to use education data to: Support students Improve school access Inform policy decisions Evaluate educational outcomes 5. Collaboration Between School Systems The fellowship explores ways to improve collaboration between: Public school districts Charter schools Education agencies Community organizations 6. Addressing Enrollment Decline Participants develop strategies for responding to: Declining student populations Resource allocation challenges School planning Equity-centered enrollment policies 7. School Performance Measurement The fellowship also examines methods for creating: More accurate school performance measures Fair accountability systems Better educational evaluation frameworks 8. Selective School Admissions Participants discuss equitable approaches to: Seat allocation Admissions policies Access to selective schools 9. User-Friendly Enrollment Systems The programme helps Fellows design enrollment systems that are: Accessible Transparent Easy for families to navigate Inclusive for diverse communities Fellowship Programming The SAQ Fellowship combines in-person experiences with virtual learning throughout the year. In-Person Programming Two-Day Kickoff at MIT The fellowship begins with a two-day event hosted at MIT. Participants: Meet fellow cohort members Explore key education policy issues Build relationships Begin collaborative learning City Learning Visit Fellows also participate in a two-day immersive visit to another city where they study real-world enrollment and school performance practices. This allows participants to observe innovative education systems and learn directly from local practitioners. Virtual Programming Throughout the year, Fellows participate in a variety of online learning opportunities. Monthly Challenge Sessions Participants work together on case studies and discuss practical solutions to real enrollment and school performance challenges. Webinar Series Leading researchers and policy experts deliver presentations covering: Education policy Enrollment systems School performance Equity Artificial Intelligence Expert Office Hours Fellows receive personalized support through one-on-one meetings with enrollment specialists and research experts. Capstone Project Each Fellow completes an individual project during the programme. At the end of the fellowship, participants present their work and lessons learned to the cohort. Ongoing Virtual Community The fellowship maintains active engagement through: Monthly Newsletters Participants receive regular updates featuring: Education news Research Resources Event summaries Policy developments Online Learning Portal Current Fellows and alumni share: Resources Best practices Research Collaboration opportunities Who Can Become a Fellow? The fellowship is designed for professionals working in education leadership roles. Participants typically come from: Public school districts State education agencies Charter management organizations Nonprofit organizations Their diverse professional experiences enrich discussions and strengthen collaborative learning. Alumni Community Participation extends beyond the one-year programme. Graduates become members of an active alumni network and are encouraged to continue participating in: Events Knowledge sharing Professional collaboration Fellowship activities This lifelong network enables continued learning and partnership among education leaders. Why Focus on School Enrollment and Performance? MIT highlights several pressing challenges facing education today. These include: Nationwide declines in public school enrollment Increasing student disengagement Persistent inequities in school access Limited access to accurate school quality information Despite these challenges, enrollment systems remain one of the most powerful tools for improving educational equity. The fellowship equips participants with the research, knowledge, and practical skills needed to redesign these systems in ways that better serve students, families, and communities. Benefits of the Fellowship Participants benefit from numerous professional development opportunities, including: One-year leadership development programme Access to MIT researchers and education experts Peer learning with education leaders nationwide Two-day kickoff event at MIT Two-day city learning visit Monthly challenge sessions Webinar series Individual expert office hours Capstone project Monthly education newsletters Online collaboration platform Lifelong alumni network Practical AI and education policy training Opportunities to exchange ideas with leaders across education sectors Application Deadline Applications for the MIT School Access and Quality Fellowship are currently open. Application Deadline: 24 August 2026 at 5:00 PM ET Interested applicants should submit their applications before the deadline. How to Apply Prospective applicants should complete the official online application through the MIT School Access and Quality Fellowship webpage. Applicants are encouraged to: Review the fellowship objectives. Confirm that their professional role aligns with the programme. Prepare any required application materials. Submit their application before 24 August 2026 at 5:00 PM ET . Learn more about applying APPLY HERE Frequently Asked Questions What is the Fellowship s timeline? The Fellowship starts with an in-person Kickoff event in the fall. It concludes in early summer with the City Learning Visit and a written reflection of each Fellow’s accomplishments. When and where are the events? The location of the in-person events varies by cohort. Fellows will be polled and notified of the event dates and locations in advance. Some events may be hybrid or virtual only. What are some examples of past topics? In recent cohorts, we have covered many topics, such as how to: improve equity in Fellows’ cities, use enrollment data to drive decision-making, develop more equitable and accurate school quality measures, engage the community to foster equitable enrollment, increase access to early childhood education, unify enrollment for after-school programs, improve relationships between districts and charters, address declining enrollment, and more. What if my region hasn’t yet started unified enrollment? Everyone is welcome to join. We think that the diversity in current enrollment practices is an asset to this Fellowship – Fellows can learn from one another about potential challenges and opportunities. What is the estimated time commitment as a Fellow? Fellows are expected to attend a two day Kickoff, a two-day City Learning Visit, two hour-long webinars (out of three), and monthly challenge sessions. Fellows are also expected to dedicate several hours throughout the Fellowship to completing a capstone project of their choosing and preparing a short presentation on their efforts. Fellows will also submit a summary of accomplishments upon the conclusion of the program. Who do I contact with questions? Please reach out to tgerstle@mitblueprintlabs.org with any questions. Is there any financial obligation associated with the Fellowship? There is no fee associated with the Fellowship, though Fellows (or their organizations) are expected to cover the costs of travel and lodging for both in-person events. Five travel scholarships are available based on need and merit to cover up to $1,200 in travel and lodging expenses for each event. What is the capstone project? Fellows will commit to a project of their choosing related to enrollment or school performance (e.g., implementing a new school quality measure, pursuing an enrollment policy change). Periodically, Fellows will report on their progress, culminating in a 5-minute presentation about their accomplishments at the end of the year. Source: https://blueprintlabs.mit.edu/apply-to-the-school-access-and-quality-fellowship/ Why You Should Apply The MIT School Access and Quality Fellowship offers an exceptional opportunity for education leaders seeking to improve equity in school enrollment and performance systems. Rather than focusing solely on theory, the fellowship provides practical strategies, collaborative learning experiences, and direct access to leading researchers and policy experts. Participants gain valuable insights into AI-enabled education systems, data-informed decision-making, and evidence-based policies that can improve educational opportunities for students nationwide. For professionals committed to building fairer, more inclusive education systems, this fellowship provides the knowledge, network, and leadership development needed to drive meaningful change. Visit HERE to learn more about the MIT School Access and Quality Fellowship. Conclusion The MIT School Access and Quality Fellowship 2026–2027 is an outstanding professional development opportunity for education leaders working to create more equitable school enrollment systems and improve school performance policies. Through a year-long combination of in-person events, virtual learning, expert mentorship, collaborative problem-solving, and research-informed discussions, Fellows develop practical skills that can transform educational access and outcomes in their communities. By examining pressing challenges such as declining enrollment, school accountability, family engagement, and the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence in education, the fellowship prepares participants to lead innovative and equitable reforms. Those working within public education systems, charter organizations, state education agencies, and nonprofit organizations are encouraged to apply before the 24 August 2026 at 5:00 PM ET deadline to become part of this distinguished network of education leaders. title: Research Assistant – U.S. Immigration Policy Program at the Migration Policy Institute (MPI): Apply for a Policy Research Career in Washington, D.C.
summary: If you are passionate about immigration policy, public policy research, legal and regulatory analysis, and evidence-based policymaking, the Migration Policy Institute (MPI) is offering an outstanding opportunity to advance your career. About the Migration Policy Institute (MPI) The Migration Policy Institute (MPI) is an independent, nonpartisan think tank dedicated to improving immigration and integration policies through rigorous research, objective analysis, policy dialogue, and innovative solutions. MPI has built an international reputation for producing authoritative research on migration and immigration issues affecting governments, institutions, and communities around the world. Rather than advocating for political positions, the institute focuses on producing evidence-based research that helps policymakers make informed decisions. The organization values: Independent and objective research Policy innovation Diversity of thought Inclusive workplaces Evidence-based decision-making Professional excellence MPI is also deeply committed to creating an equitable workplace where employees from diverse backgrounds, experiences, and perspectives are welcomed and supported. This is an excellent opportunity for someone seeking long-term professional growth in policy research, immigration studies, public affairs, or legal analysis. Working closely with senior researchers, the successful candidate will help monitor rapidly changing immigration developments while contributing to publications that reach policymakers and national audiences.
